questions.question_text: Derive the identity relating $\tan\alpha$ and $\sec\alpha$ from $\cos^{2}\alpha+\sin^{2}\alpha=1$ by dividing through by $\cos^{2}\alpha$, where $\cos\alpha\neq 0$. Select the complete correct derivation.

options.why: Replaced $\dfrac{\sin^{2}\alpha}{\cos^{2}\alpha}$ with $\cot^{2}\alpha$ instead of $\tan^{2}\alpha$.
Divided the terms on the left by $\cos^{2}\alpha$ but left the right-hand side unchanged.
Replaced $\dfrac{1}{\cos^{2}\alpha}$ with $\sec\alpha$, dropping the square.

questions.question_text: Which identity results from dividing $\cos^{2}\theta+\sin^{2}\theta=1$ through by $\sin^{2}\theta$ (where $\sin\theta\neq 0$)?

options.why: This identity results from dividing by $\cos^2\theta$, not $\sin^2\theta$.
Subtracted $1$ instead of adding $1$ when evaluating $\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta}=1$.
Confused the ratio $\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$ with $\tan\theta$ and rearranged incorrectly.
Factored out $3$ but dropped the coefficient from the final expression.
Replaced $1-\sin^2 x$ with $\tan^2 x$ instead of $\cos^2 x$.
Incorrectly replaced $\sin^{2}x$ with $-\cos^{2}x$, giving $3-3(-\cos^{2}x)=3+3\cos^{2}x$.
Evaluated $\operatorname{cosec}^2\alpha - \cot^2\alpha$ instead of $\cot^2\alpha - \operatorname{cosec}^2\alpha$.
Replaced cotangent and cosecant difference with tangent.
Assumed $\cot^2\alpha$ and $\operatorname{cosec}^2\alpha$ are equal.
Interchanged sine and cosine in the given expression, simplifying $5\sin^{2}\theta(1-\cos^{2}\theta)=5\sin^{4}\theta$ instead.
Factored out $5$ but dropped the coefficient from the final simplified expression.
Factored correctly as $5\cos^{2}\theta(1-\sin^{2}\theta)$ but incorrectly replaced $1-\sin^{2}\theta$ with $\sin^{2}\theta$.
Incorrectly replaced $1+\cot^{2}\theta$ with $\sec^{2}\theta$, giving $\sec^{2}\theta\sin^{2}\theta=\dfrac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta}=\tan^{2}\theta$.
Incorrectly replaced $1+\cot^{2}\theta$ with $\sec^{2}\theta$ and then omitted the remaining factor $\sin^{2}\theta$.
Omitted the $1 \times \sin^2\theta$ term when expanding the brackets.

questions.question_text: Prove $\dfrac{1-\sin\alpha}{\cos^{2}\alpha}=\dfrac{1}{1+\sin\alpha}$, where $\cos\alpha\neq 0$, by simplifying the left-hand side to match the right-hand side. Select the complete correct proof.

options.why: Incorrectly factorised $1-\sin^{2}\alpha$ as $(1-\sin\alpha)^{2}$ and claimed that $\dfrac{1}{1-\sin\alpha}$ matches the right-hand side.
Incorrectly replaced $\cos^{2}\alpha$ with $1-\sin\alpha$ rather than $1-\sin^{2}\alpha$, then claimed that $1$ matches the right-hand side.
After cancelling $1-\sin\alpha$, moved the remaining denominator into the numerator, giving $1+\sin\alpha$ instead of its reciprocal.
Split the expression as $3-\dfrac{3}{\sec^{2}\theta}=3-3\cos^{2}\theta$ but retained only the magnitude of the subtracted term, $3\cos^{2}\theta$.
Evaluated the numerator $3\tan^2\theta$ but omitted the division by $\sec^2\theta$.
Assumed $\frac{3\sec^2\theta-3}{\sec^2\theta}=3-3=0$ without algebraic separation.
Added the square of $(2+3)$ instead of expanding the binomials and using $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$.
Added the coefficients $2+3$ rather than summing the squared coefficients $4+9$.
Failed to cancel the cross terms $+12\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and $-12\sin\theta\cos\theta$.
Uses the reciprocal cosine expression rather than the corresponding secant identity.
Drops the square even though the identity produces a squared tangent.
The standard Pythagorean identity gives a matching option, namely squared tangent.

questions.solution_text: Using $\sec^2(\theta)=1+\tan^2(\theta)$, subtracting $1$ from both sides gives $\sec^2(\theta)-1=\tan^2(\theta)$.
